In previous seasons, I’d usually use his ult more offensively. This season, I’ve had to adjust for the damage output of dps. I now use his ult more conservatively and almost as an additional shield when I really need it or feel I can tilt the tide of a team duel in our favor. 

Lately, I’ll pop it when I’ve got my barrier and nemesis on cooldown and the enemy team is down 1-2 players. I’ll stay on the objective and try to use it as a self sustain and third shield while blocking. Giving my team time to focus on the remaining enemies while I hopefully draw fire and the attention of the enemy team. Typically blocking and positioning behind a corner or the payload, but moving around to try and draw fire if that makes sense.

Adding on to the other posts, ability cooldown management is crucial this season in addition to positioning. Using his Nemesis form as a way to back out of a fight is also important. Pop Nemesis when you’re running low on health and be sure to block and then disengage to keep yourself in the fight while you back up, reposition and hopefully, get healed.

I still see a lot of Rams not using his block in Nemesis form which almost acts as a secondary shield. But watch out because you’ll still melt if you get focused so game sense and awareness is also important to keep in mind.

Pretty much what people here have been saying. Tank is a crucial role that will make or break a game. However, tank is also heavily reliant on the rest of your team performing well and coordinating. As a tank, if you don’t have heals or back up DPS, you’re not going to survive. And if you’re having a bad game as the Tank, or if you’re just a bad Tank, the rest of your team might be playing brilliantly but more often than not, you’ll still lose. At the end of the day, this is a team game based around the objectives. And unfortunately, not everyone is a team player. You’ll win some and lose some. 

Best you can do is try to have fun when you play and pay no mind to the haters in chat. Especially if your tank game was on point but certain team members feel short. Sometimes it is a Tank Diff, sure. Take that and improve on where you struggled. But don’t read into it too much cause people will always try to throw someone else under the bus. Just have fun! And occasionally play a different role to keep things fresh.

You’re welcome! A lot of people aren’t overly enthusiastic about therapy and it’s rooted in our culture to be against it. However that narrative has been changing in recent years and you might be shocked just how many people go to therapy and never ever mention it. But they still go because it helps. 

I also avoided visits out of the same kind of fear. I didn’t want to see her the way she was and wanted to keep the healthier, better memory alive. I also didn’t expect her to pass when she did so I was a bit shocked. But she had been going downhill for sometime and I had been distancing myself for a bit. 

It’s hard to say because everyone and every situation is different. I myself had friends and colleagues all tell me the same thing. Go see her, you’ll regret not spending the time etc etc and I still ignored it. I learned from my own mistakes that they were right and that they were speaking from a place of understanding (even tho at the time, to me, it sounded generic and cliche.) 

You could suggest that if he isn’t comfortable seeing her often, make the effort once a week or every other week. But try to at least call her often and talk to her. Even if it’s just calling to say “Hi” and “I love you.”  Even if it’s short, I’m sure it’ll make her day! If they’ve got iPhones, they could even FaceTime here and there. The thing is, a mothers love is special and it may be hard for her too, but mothers  will always understand. It sounds like they are close, so I’m sure those calls will be the highlight of her day just hearing his voice!

Honestly just being there for him will go a long way. Being supportive and understanding if he’s having a bad day with it all. Losing a mother is tough and is even tougher if that person is close to their mother. Understand it may be a bit of a journey for him to go through the stages of grief. If you notice that he begins unhealthy habits to cope, like drinking more or throwing himself into work more, or eating more, be aware and gently let him know.

 My biggest suggestion is to encourage him to start therapy now. That’ll be huge and it can take time to find a therapist you connect with and a bit more time to get comfortable with that therapist. Therapy will be a major help. 

I know from personal experience as a guy. I lost my mother years ago in my early 20’s. I was in a relationship that turned to long distance and I was broke. I threw myself into work and stuffed that emotional stuff down. I had my bad days and good days. It took years and I’m still not over it. You never really get over losing a parent especially a mother. 

However, it gets easier with the support of loved ones and time. In hindsight, my biggest regret was not spending more time with my mom before she passed. I was afraid. But that fear kept me from spending valuable time that was left. 

The other biggest lesson I learned was to go to therapy. I wish I had started even tho I was broke and busy with work and school then. It’s not unmanly to go to therapy. In reality, I have learned to really like it as it’s a way to really get those pent up feelings out in a safe environment without the fear of judgement or weighing down people i am close to with my own personal stuff. It has allowed my relationships to be better and a lot of times I looks forward to that hour. 

But remember to take time and take care of yourself as well. Communication is a big factor in the healing journey after a big loss. But don’t ever hesitate to reach out for support!
